findings.heading: fill()
findings.proposition: The French prose names the function to apply as `pivot_larger()`, while the chunk immediately below calls `pivot_wider()` and the English names no function at all.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader looks for a function called pivot_larger(), which does not exist in tidyr; typing it returns 'could not find function "pivot_larger"' and the reader cannot connect the sentence to the pivot_wider() call in the chunk.

findings.heading: Pivoting data of multiple classes
findings.proposition: The English says the special term ".value" makes the pivoted columns split on a CHARACTER in their name; the French says they are split on the basis of a WORD ("un mot") in the column name.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader concludes names_sep takes a word rather than a single separator character, and may pass "date"/"status" or a multi-character token to names_sep = instead of the underscore, producing a failed or wrongly-named pivot.

findings.heading: Pivoting data of multiple classes
findings.proposition: The English states that after the naive pivot the utility of the dates is lost; the French states only that the function converts the whole column to character and omits the consequence for the dates.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader sees the class coercion as a cosmetic type change and misses the reason the whole section exists: date arithmetic, sorting and date-scaled plotting no longer work on that column.

findings.heading: "Wide" format
findings.proposition: The French adds that the count columns comprise one column per age class plus one column for the day's total in that facility, and concludes that the case-count information therefore sits across several columns rather than one, 'hence the so-called wide structure'; the English segment states none of this.
findings.reader_consequence: None harmful: the added definition is correct for this dataset, but the French reader meets the totals column and the definition of 'wide' one paragraph earlier than the English reader, so the two texts diverge in what has been established at this point.

findings.heading: "Wide" format
findings.proposition: The English hedges that wide format 'may be useful for presentation' and 'is not ideal for SOME TYPES of analysis'; the French asserts that it is useful for data entry and presentation and is not appropriate for MANY analyses ('de nombreuses analyses').
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader takes a stronger prohibition on wide data than the English gives, and may pivot data that would have been fine to analyse as-is.

findings.heading: Standard pivoting
findings.proposition: The English says the resulting plot is a STACKED bar chart; the French says only 'un diagramme en batons' (a bar chart) and drops 'stacked'.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader is not told that fill = age_group stacks the age groups within each bar, which is the exact property that makes the doubled bar height in the next paragraph visible and explicable.
